entities.description:

entities.description:

entities.description:
Within one sample, Δ = X̄ − μ does not depend on the observation index i. Its square is therefore also index-independent.
Use c = Δ² in the rule for summing a constant: the same value is added n times.
Δ is still random across repeated samples. Being constant with respect to i does not make it fixed across samples.

entities.description:
Now pass from a within-sample identity to a statement about repeated sampling.
Take expectations on both sides and use linearity on the residual-square sum plus the shared-shift term.

entities.description:
About the fixed population mean, each observation has expected squared deviation σ². The finite sum therefore has expectation nσ².

entities.description:

scenes.narration: A mean describes a center, but not the variation around that center. This lecture develops measures of spread from observed residuals, explains why estimating the mean changes variance estimation, and connects variation of sample means to random uncertainty. The practical interpretation always depends on what was measured and which sampling assumptions are justified.

scenes.narration:

A report containing only their common mean would conceal this difference. We therefore need a quantity that describes the distances between the observations and their center.

Such comparisons require consistent units and stated measurement conditions. scenes.narration: A residual is an observed value minus the mean of the same observations. Residuals retain the measurement unit and indicate both direction and distance: negative values fall below the fitted mean, and positive values above it. We can calculate all these quantities from the sample, without knowing the population mean. Signed residuals alone do not provide a useful total measure of spread because they cancel.

scenes.narration:
Squaring each residual makes every contribution nonnegative, so opposite signs no longer cancel. The sum of squared residuals increases when observations lie farther from their fitted center.

items.text: MSD describes the average squared deviation per observation.

scenes.narration: The mean squared deviation, MSD, is the sum of squared residuals divided by the number of observations. It is a descriptive summary of this particular sample around its own fitted mean. Series A and Series B have the same center, but different MSD values. Describing the observed sample and estimating an unknown population variance are related tasks, not identical definitions.

items.text: MSD describes this observed sample around its fitted mean. Lowercase xᵢ and x̄ are realized values.
Variance describes the underlying random variable around its expectation. The generally unknown σ² is our estimation target.

scenes.narration:
The empirical MSD is calculated from lowercase observed values and their sample mean. In contrast, the theoretical variance is the expected squared distance of a random measurement $X$ from its expectation $\mu$.

The expectation is a probability-weighted theoretical average, not a guarantee about one finite dataset. The generally unknown population variance $\sigma^2$ is the quantity we would like to estimate from observations.

Expectation leaves a fixed constant unchanged, responds linearly to fixed scaling and shifting, and distributes over a fixed finite sum. The required expectations must exist; independence is not needed for this finite linearity.

A useful long-run interpretation comes from the law of large numbers: for independent identically distributed observations with a finite expected absolute value, their sample average converges to the population expectation. A finite observed average can still differ from it.

scenes.narration:
A fixed constant has zero variance. Adding a fixed shift does not change spread, whereas scaling a random quantity by $a$ multiplies its variance by $a^2$.

For a sum of two random quantities, the general identity includes twice their covariance. Covariance is the expected product of their centered deviations. With finite second moments, independence implies zero covariance, but zero covariance does not generally imply independence.

A single MSD may lie above or below the true variance. Simulated averages approximate an expectation but do not by themselves establish a mathematical identity.

explanation.text:
In the general factorization use a = σ².
The fraction left after subtraction is (n−1)/n, strictly less than one for n > 1. Thus the MSD is biased downward when σ² > 0.
A particular realized MSD may lie above or below σ². Bias is the repeated-sampling expectation, not the direction of every individual error.

from.label: Insert the expected squared error, not an observed shift

steps.operation: Factor out the population variance

rule.description: Write a as na/n, subtract a/n and factor out a. The result holds for every real a and positive integer n. This is algebra, not an additional statistical assumption.
rule.label: Factor a common value

to.label: The MSD bias factor

blocks.spokenText: From the fitted-mean identity to unbiased variance

items.text: Insert Var(X̄) = σ²/n into E[MSDₙ] = σ² − Var(X̄), then factor the common σ².
The downward bias factor is (n−1)/n in expectation, not in every sample. The model assumptions of the preceding result still apply.

scenes.narration:
Substitute the sample-mean variance into the expected MSD identity. Subtracting $\sigma^2/n$ from $\sigma^2$ leaves $(n-1)\sigma^2/n$.

Thus the MSD underestimates the population variance in expectation by the factor $(n-1)/n$ under the stated sampling assumptions. This is an average-bias statement, not a promise that every observed MSD will be smaller than the population variance.

legend.description: Corrected variance statistic; s² is its observed value.

explanation.text: Define the random statistic S² by multiplying MSDₙ by the fixed reciprocal n/(n−1). Linearity moves that coefficient outside E and the factors cancel. S² is unbiased under the stated assumptions. Its observed value s² is not generally exactly σ², and the square root is not automatically unbiased.

steps.operation: Multiply by the reciprocal bias factor, for n > 1

rule.description: A constant fixed across repeated samples multiplies the expectation. A random offset such as Δ must not itself be pulled outside E; the fixed count n may be.
rule.label: Factor a fixed constant out of expectation

to.label: Correct the systematic bias from fitting the same sample mean

scenes.narration:
For $n>1$, multiply the MSD statistic by the reciprocal bias factor $n/(n-1)$. Linearity of expectation then gives a corrected statistic with expectation $\sigma^2$.

The correction compensates for estimating the center from the same observations. It does not remove the random variation between individual samples, and taking the square root of an unbiased variance estimator does not automatically give an unbiased standard-deviation estimator.

items.text: S² denotes the statistic across samples; s² is its observed value. The practical formula needs only xᵢ, x̄ and n > 1, not the unknown μ or σ².
Unbiasedness means the correct average over hypothetical samples. One realized s² need not equal the population variance.

scenes.narration:
In practice, calculate the corrected sample variance by dividing the observed sum of squared residuals by $n-1$. The uppercase statistic $S^2$ varies across hypothetical samples; lowercase $s^2$ denotes the value calculated from the observed data.

This practical formula requires the observations, their fitted mean and a sample size greater than one, but no knowledge of $\mu$ or $\sigma^2$. Its unbiasedness remains conditional on the sampling assumptions.

scenes.narration: The expectation calculation explains the Monte Carlo shortfall. The chart compares the original simulated MSD averages, their paired corrected averages, and the theoretical expected MSD curve. Agreement of the simulation with theory is a useful numerical check. It remains important to distinguish finite simulated averages from exact theoretical expectations and to retain the same underlying sampling model when comparing them.

Apply Bessel's correction to Series A and B. Both means are $32/3$ mg/L. Their squared-residual totals are $26/3$ and $218/3$ $(\mathrm{mg/L})^2$, respectively.

With three observations, the corrected divisor is two, giving sample variances $13/3$ and $109/3$ $(\mathrm{mg/L})^2$. The calculation illustrates the same estimator for differently dispersed samples without requiring either unknown population variance.

explanation.text:
Series A has sample variance 13/3 (mg/L)².
Take its nonnegative square root: √(13/3) ≈ 2.081666, reported here as 2.082 mg/L. The concentration unit is no longer squared.
This is a root-mean-square measure of residual size with the stated divisor, not an arithmetic mean of absolute distances.

rule.description: Standard deviation is the nonnegative square root of variance. Taking the square root also restores the original physical unit. It is not the mean absolute deviation, and an unbiased variance estimate does not imply an unbiased square root.

to.label: Standard deviation on the concentration scale

items.text: Concentration → Variance → Standard deviation: mg/L → (mg/L)² → mg/L.
SD restores the measurement scale. It is not the mean absolute deviation from the sample mean.

scenes.narration: Standard deviation is the square root of variance. The result returns to the original measurement unit and is therefore easier to compare with measured concentrations. A larger sample SD indicates greater observed spread under the stated conditions. The square root is a separate nonlinear transformation: unbiasedness of sample variance is not transferred automatically to the sample SD.

Read the sample SD formula as a sequence of operations: center each observation at the sample mean, square the residuals, sum them, apply the corrected divisor $n-1$, and take the square root. The sample size must exceed one.

This describes sample spread in the original unit; it does not by itself state uncertainty of a mean or establish agreement with a reference value.

The SD is expressed in mg/L, whereas variance is in $(\mathrm{mg/L})^2$. These are summaries of the same observed samples, not new measurement data or a direct determination of population parameters.

scenes.narration: The independent experimental unit depends on what is repeated. Three injections of one vial repeat instrumental operations, but share the preparation and field sample. items.text: **Earlier:** this term explained the gap between E[MSDₙ] and σ² when we fitted the mean.
**Now:** Var(X̄) describes how sample means scatter around μ over repeated samples. It is ==uncertainty information about the estimated mean==, not the known error of this one result.

scenes.narration:
Earlier, $\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\sigma^2/n$ explained the difference between the expected MSD and the population variance when the same sample was used to fit the mean.

The same term has a second interpretation: it describes how sample means vary around $\mu$ across repeated samples. It therefore provides information about random uncertainty of the estimated mean. It does not reveal the actual error of the one realized sample mean.

Variance can describe data or quantify uncertainty of an estimator, including later model parameters. ==s/√n applies to this mean, not every estimator==. Correlation and systematic effects need separate treatment.

scenes.narration:
To make the estimator notation distinct, now call the same measurement variable $Y$ and its sample mean $\bar Y$. This is a local renaming, not a change in the observations or sampling model.

The SD $\sigma$ describes individual measurements; the standard error of $\bar Y$ is the square root of its sampling variance, $\sigma/\sqrt n$. When $\sigma$ is unknown, $s/\sqrt n$ estimates that SE.

Variance can quantify estimator uncertainty as well as descriptive spread, but this particular formula is not universal for arbitrary model parameters.

items.text: **Square-root law:** at fixed population spread, four times as many independent observations halve the SE. Individual measurement spread does not shrink.
**Scope:** independent observations with common finite variance. Correlation or systematic bias can leave ==uncertainty that averaging does not remove==.

scenes.narration:
At fixed population SD and under the stated independent common finite-variance sampling assumptions, the standard error decreases in proportion to $1/\sqrt n$. Four times as many independent observations halve the SE, and the theoretical SE tends to zero as $n\to\infty$.

Individual measurement spread does not shrink. Correlated readings and systematic effects may leave uncertainty that averaging does not remove, so this limiting result does not imply vanishing total measurement uncertainty.

scenes.narration:
For the five QC A measurements, the observed mean is 10.00 mg/L, the sample variance is $0.025\,(\mathrm{mg/L})^2$, and the SD is approximately 0.1581 mg/L. Assuming iid repeats, the estimated SE of $\bar Y$ is 0.0707 mg/L.

A rounded report is therefore $(10.00\pm0.07)\,\mathrm{mg/L}$, explicitly mean plus or minus one estimated SE with $n=5$. Error bars must state what they represent: this is neither an SD bar nor a 95% confidence interval or a complete uncertainty budget.

MSD describes the sample around its fitted center, while the corrected sample variance estimates population variance under explicit assumptions. SD returns to the original unit, and RSD describes relative spread only on a suitable scale. Precision requires stated conditions and cannot establish trueness.
